He was really kind, understanding, and eager to teach. He answered all of our questions and provided both an answer and a different way to solve the question. His solutions were detailed enough.  Still, I sometimes had difficulties understanding what he was trying to teach. If I knew the topic or practiced beforehand, I had no trouble understanding it; but if it was a topic that I was not familiar with, I had a hard time following the lecture. Some lectures were not efficient. One of the main reasons was that the questions were not clear enough. He was solving someting, but I generally found myself thinking what the question wanted in the first place. Wrtiting the questions on the board my be a waste of time, but he can specifically state the questions that we will be solving from the past exams or share us a document of the questions that we will be solving in class before the lecture. This way I can come to the class prepared, and focus on the solutions better by connecting the question with the solutions. I found his office hours to be effective. He helped me a lot by explaining what I did not understand.

There is a lot to say about Yiğit Hoca. Unfortunately, none is positive. For all the courses I have taken that are worth several years of my life, I haven't seen such awful homework and quizzes. Sometimes, there is literally no question asked in them, so you are just expected to stare at the walls of texts to make the non-existent question solvable. Sometimes, he provides a code that is just not working, and you have to rework it to reinvent the homework question itself. There are several reasons for the codes to not work, such as having a function defined in the middle of the Python code, the code iterating a 3D array with 2D arrays, or, my favorite, "there is no functionality called x inside the library y." I suspect he uses ChatGPT to write these brilliant "codes." There is one thing I have learned in this course, and it is how to deal with incompetent superiors.
